messages.subject: problems with multiple group SEM
parts:
Dear all
I have data from an experiment, where I have 5 groups, each having around 45 participants. I have measured three constructs, before and after the experiment. Each construct has around 5 indicators. I want to compare the five groups but when I run the analysis I get the usual error that the sample size is too small for the estimation of the gamma. Thus, I decided to drop the multigroup SEM and instead use the groups as dummy variables in regressions to predict the change in the factors before and after... any examples I can review/follow?
Thank you for your time
Iasonas

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: problems with multiple group SEM
parts: I decided to drop the multigroup SEM and instead use the groups as dummy variables in regressions to predict the change in the factors before and after... any examples I can review/follow?

MIMIC (http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00273170802620121) models assume measurement equivalence just like multigroup models do.  Invariance of item intercepts can be evaluated in the MIMIC framework (with the additional assumption of homogeneous residual variances) but is complicated by the need to choose at least one anchor item that is assumed to be DIF-free.  Woods (2009: http://apm.sagepub.com/content/33/1/42) describes a pretty good method for empirically selecting anchors.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: problems with multiple group SEM
parts: is better to use the groups as dummy variables to run an anova-style analysis in regressions, rather than use a multiple-group SEM.

Oh, if you are forming a composite from the 5 indicators, then they can be treated as continuous, so estimating a multigroup path analysis  with ML would probably not return an error.  The multigroup approach allows you to relax the assumption of homogeneity of variances across groups, and I find it much more intuitive to test equivalence of slopes across groups by constraining them to equality than by complicating a single-group model with several dummy codes and interaction terms.  

Chapter 24 of Hoyle's (2012) Handbook of SEM is a great chapter to read about doing ANOVA/regression type analyses with multigroup SEM.  It's more focused on comparing means (the slopes of dummy codes), but similar principles apply for slopes of continuous variables.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
